name: South Deering Sump
description:
South Deering Sump is where GLMZ keeps its worst secrets, sealed under contaminated water and abandoned industrial infrastructure. The original South Deering was already haunted before the collapse — the Wisconsin Steel plant closure in 1980 was one of the most brutal in American industrial history, three thousand workers losing their jobs in a single day with no warning and no severance, their pension fund looted by management. The land the plant stood on was so contaminated that remediation estimates exceeded the property value by a factor of ten. Nobody cleaned it up. Nobody ever does.

When the Calumet River's water levels rose, the contaminated industrial sites along its banks didn't just flood — they dissolved. Decades of industrial waste that had been sitting in soil and slag heaps entered the water column, creating a toxic soup that now fills the low-lying areas of the former industrial zone. The Sump, as locals call it, is a landscape of half-submerged factory ruins standing in water that changes color depending on what the current is stirring up. Orange means iron compounds. Green means copper salts. Black means don't ask. The water is warm in places where underground chemical reactions are still running, steam rising from the surface on cold mornings like breath from a sleeping industrial corpse.

Axiom classified South Deering Sump as an exclusion zone — corporate territory in name, abandoned in practice, maintained at the minimum level required to prevent contamination from spreading to adjacent districts. This means a perimeter fence, monitoring stations that are checked quarterly, and a total absence of residential services. But people live here anyway, because people live everywhere that institutions abandon. The Sump's population consists of the truly excluded — those whose tier status is so far below the floor that even the Shelf won't have them. They live in the upper floors of factory ruins, above the waterline, in conditions that no one with options would accept. They fish the contaminated water for mutated species that they eat because the alternative is not eating.

The Sump's value, such as it is, lies in its toxicity. Nobody comes here willingly, which makes it an effective hiding place for things that need hiding. Smugglers use the flooded factory complexes as warehouses — the contamination keeps casual intruders out and the Axiom exclusion zone classification keeps corporate security from patrolling beyond the perimeter. The Calumet River provides water access to South Calumet, Old Harbor, and eventually Lake Michigan. And beneath the water, in the sealed vaults of the old Wisconsin Steel administrative complex, there are records — personnel files, financial documents, corporate communications — that were never digitized because the company died before the digital transition and nobody thought paper records at the bottom of a toxic lake were worth recovering. Someone might think differently now.

sights: Half-submerged factory ruins rising from discolored water — industrial cathedrals slowly being consumed
Water that shifts color by the hour: orange, green, iridescent black, depending on subsurface chemistry
Steam rising from warm spots where underground chemical reactions continue decades after operations ceased
The perimeter fence, more symbolic than functional, its warning signs faded to illegibility
Improvised shelters in factory upper floors, lights visible through broken industrial windows after dark
Mutated aquatic life visible in the shallows — oversized, discolored, moving in ways that suggest adaptation to something
sounds: Water moving through industrial ruins — a gurgling, echoing sound unique to flooded structures
Chemical reactions bubbling to the surface in the warm zones, a low persistent fizz
The creak of metal structures under water stress, factory skeletons shifting on their foundations
Quiet — the Sump is one of the quietest places in Meridian because almost no one is here
Occasionally, the sound of a hull moving through water — smugglers navigating the flooded channels
smells: Chemical contamination — sharp, metallic, with an organic undertone that suggests biological processes nobody wants to study
Rust and decay — the smell of industrial infrastructure returning to its constituent elements
Steam from the warm zones carrying a sulfurous edge
Nothing clean — the Sump has no clean smell. Every breath carries a reminder of what was done here.
atmosphere.feel: South Deering Sump feels like guilt made physical. This is what happens when industry takes everything from a place and then leaves the corpse for someone else to deal with. The contamination is not an accident or a tragedy — it's a ledger entry, a cost that was calculated, accepted, and externalized onto people who couldn't refuse it. Living here means breathing that calculation every day.

demographics: Population estimates range from 2,000 to 5,000, though no census has been attempted. Entirely untier-ed or functionally Tier 0. The most marginalized population in GLMZ — those with nowhere else to go. Mixed origins, united by exclusion.
economy: Subsistence fishing in contaminated water. Smuggling infrastructure — warehouse space in the flooded factories, water route access via the Calumet River. Salvage operations in the industrial ruins, extracting metals and materials that retain value despite contamination. No formal economy exists.
power_structure: No governance. Axiom's exclusion zone classification means the district exists on paper as corporate territory with no corporate presence. Informal authority belongs to whoever controls the most functional factory shelter and the best water access points. Smuggling operations bring external power dynamics into the Sump on a transactional basis.
dangers: Toxic exposure — the water, the air, the soil are all contaminated, and the health effects are cumulative and severe
Structural collapse — flooded factory ruins are structurally unpredictable and fail without warning
Isolation — the Sump is far from medical care, mutual aid networks, and emergency response of any kind
The things in the water — mutated aquatic life that has adapted to the contamination and doesn't always avoid humans
Smuggling operations attract attention that the Sump's vulnerable population cannot defend against
The contamination itself is not stable — chemical reactions continue underground, and sudden toxic releases have occurred
opportunities: The flooded factory complexes provide unmonitored warehouse space accessible by water
Calumet River access connects to the broader southern waterway network
The Wisconsin Steel administrative vault contains undigitized records that may have significant intelligence value
The Sump's exclusion zone status means Axiom security does not patrol inside the perimeter — an increasingly rare condition in Meridian
Environmental contamination data, properly documented, could support legal action against Axiom or its predecessor entities
story_hooks: A salvage diver working the Wisconsin Steel ruins has found the sealed administrative vault and realized the paper records inside are intact. She can't read them — they're in 20th-century corporate accounting notation — but she knows someone who can, if she can get the documents out without them dissolving in the contaminated water.

The warm zones in the Sump are getting warmer. Underground chemical reactions are accelerating, and the excluded population is reporting new symptoms — neurological, not just respiratory. Something has changed in the chemistry, and no one with the expertise to diagnose it is willing to enter the exclusion zone.

A smuggling operation has established a major waypoint in the Sump, and the traffic has attracted attention from a competing faction. The excluded population is caught in the middle, and the only person who's offered to help them is asking for something in return that they don't understand.
frequented_by: The excluded — people with no tier, no rights, and no alternative
Smugglers using the flooded factories as waypoints on the Calumet River route
Salvage operators extracting materials from the industrial ruins
Environmental researchers who enter the exclusion zone unofficially and leave with data they can't publish
No one from Axiom — the quarterly monitoring visits are conducted by drone, and the drones don't look up
